request: Check this flight: did a control fault occur, when, and where on the aircraft?

result.headline: Output ch[2] dropped to 1100 us and stayed there from t=77 s, after throttle fell to 0 at t=76 s; aircraft lost altitude.
result.explanation: A control or propulsion fault began at t=76-77 s. Throttle went to 0% and ch[2] stuck at minimum for the rest of the flight. Data cannot separate a commanded failsafe from an actuator or ESC failure on ch[2].

evidence.shows: Throttle fell from 45% to 0% and stayed at 0 for the rest of the log, with no recovery.
ch[2] went from 1480 us to 1100 us and stayed there through t=92. Other channels kept varying normally, so this one is pinned.
Relative altitude fell from about 49 m at t=76 to 26 m at t=92 with no thrust, so the aircraft was sinking.
ch[1] fell to 1180 us while ch[4] and ch[5] rose to 1640 us and pitch setpoint rose to 17.7 deg. The controller was compensating with other outputs.

effects.why: The yaw setpoint kept rising from t=77 s. The vehicle yaw followed it and altitude dropped, which looks like a consequence of lost thrust, not a separate cause.
ch[1] fell to 1180 us in the last seconds, which looks like the controller compensating for the lost ch[2] output.

next_action.action: Inspect ch[2] motor, ESC and wiring, and read the failsafe log.
next_action.why: Separates a commanded throttle cut (failsafe or low battery) from a real ch[2] actuator or ESC failure.
how: Check the controller log for a failsafe or arming-state change at t=76 s
Bench-test ch[2] output and its ESC or servo
Check battery voltage under load against the t=0.7 s low-voltage warning

outcomes.label: Failsafe or mode change logged at 76 s
outcomes.means: The throttle cut was commanded, probably by a battery or sensor failsafe.

outcomes.label: ch[2] actuator or ESC faulty on bench
outcomes.means: The ch[2] hardware failed and the output was pinned.

unknowns: Whether the throttle cut was commanded by a failsafe or came from the throttle source
What ch[2] physically drives, since it is not labelled
Why the airspeed and yaw-rate signals read 0 for the whole flight

hypotheses.claim: ch[2] output or its ESC or actuator failed or latched at minimum from t=77 s.
hypotheses.because: ch[2] is pinned at 1100 us for 16 s while the controller keeps changing the other outputs.

hypotheses.claim: Throttle was commanded to 0 at t=76 s by a failsafe, possibly from the low-voltage warning.
hypotheses.because: Throttle drops to 0 one second before ch[2] pins, and a low-voltage warning was logged at 0.7 s.

hypotheses.claim: A sensor fault (the 'Sensor helth' error, airspeed and yaw rate flat at 0) degraded control.
hypotheses.because: The sensor error appears at 0.7 s, long before the t=76-77 s change, and attitude tracking looked normal before then.

events.what: Battery low voltage warning at 0.7 s
events.why: This was logged at the start and could explain a later failsafe throttle cut.
It is consistent with the airspeed and yaw-rate channels reading 0 all flight.

events.what: Throttle to 0 at t=76 s, ch[2] pinned at 1100 us at t=77 s
events.why: This is the only abrupt change in the flight and it coincides with the loss of altitude.

events.what: Altitude falling and ch[1] diverging at the end
events.why: These follow the lost thrust and ch[2] output.

unobservable.why_it_matters: The effect of the pinned output depends on whether it is a motor or a control surface.
unobservable.how_to_observe: Check the output mapping and wiring for ch[2].
